steps.explanationAfterStep: A [1,5]-sigmatropic hydrogen shift: the H moves from carbon 1 to carbon 5 of a pentadienyl unit through a six-membered cyclic transition state. Six electrons (two π pairs and the C–H pair) move round the ring. It is suprafacial: the H stays on one face of the π system the whole way, which a small H can easily do. The product's two C=C bonds are both internal, so it is more stable. Labelling shows the H leaves and arrives on the same face. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges.

title: Suprafacial [1,5]-hydrogen shift
subtitle: (Z)-Hexa-1,3-diene becomes hexa-2,4-diene as an H moves along one face
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 35
Fleming, Pericyclic Reactions, 2nd edition (Oxford Chemistry Primers, Oxford University Press)

diene.caption: (3Z)-hexa-1,3-diene, drawn curled so the H can reach the far end
hintTiers: Number from the H: the H is atom 1 of one fragment; the carbon it leaves is atom 1 of the other, and the carbon it reaches is atom 5. Which carbon is that, and what happens to the two π bonds?
The H leaves the CH₂ next to the diene and bonds to the terminal CH₂ five carbons away; both C=C bonds move one place along. Three arrows.

Arrow 1: from the terminal C=C π bond to a new bond between the end CH₂ and the migrating H. Arrow 2: from the middle C=C π bond to the bond between the second and third carbons. Arrow 3: from the C–H bond that breaks to the bond between that carbon and its alkene neighbour.
diene.learnerPrompt: On heating, an H moves from one end of the five-carbon chain to the other. Draw the single step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That moves the H by three atoms, a [1,3] shift. A suprafacial [1,3]-H shift would need four electrons in a four-membered ring, which is not allowed thermally (and an antarafacial one is geometrically impossible). The H moves five atoms, to the end of the diene.
The methyl group stays put; it is the H on that carbon that moves.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the end of the diene takes the H. In the same step the C–H pair becomes a new C=C at the other end and the middle π bond shifts along. Two more arrows.

product.caption: hexa-2,4-diene (the new terminal methyl comes from the old CH₂=)

mechanismSummary: A sigmatropic hydrogen shift moves an H along a π system. On heating, a [1,5] shift is allowed suprafacially (six electrons, like a Diels–Alder), so the H stays on one face throughout. A thermal [1,3] shift would have to be antarafacial, which an H on a short chain cannot reach, so it is not seen; [1,7] shifts are antarafacial too, but a triene can coil into a helix and they do happen. Open-chain cis-1,3-dienes need about 200 °C. In 5-substituted cyclopenta-1,3-dienes the same [1,5] shift happens at room temperature (the H ends up on a neighbouring ring carbon), which is why such dienes must be kept cold and used quickly. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges.
